after: ## Three accounts of the rule of law
alt: Three theorists from formal to thicker. Dicey (1885): no punishment except for breach of law before the ordinary courts, everyone subject to the ordinary law, rights secured by judicial decisions. Raz (1977): a formal account in which law must be able to guide behaviour, so a system could comply and still be unjust. Bingham (2010): eight principles including human rights. A clear, prospective law that violates rights satisfies Raz but not Bingham.
caption: Raz and Bingham disagree about whether human rights belong in the rule of law.

after: ## Three accounts of the rule of law
alt: Lord Bingham’s eight principles: accessible and clear law; rights decided by law not discretion; equality except where objectively justified; officials acting in good faith and within limits; protection of fundamental human rights; civil disputes resolved without prohibitive cost or delay; fair procedures; compliance with international law. Principle 5, human rights, is highlighted.
caption: Bingham’s account goes beyond form to include rights and access to justice.

after: ## Applying the three elements: fresh authorities
alt: Three columns of authorities. No sanction except in accordance with the law: Laporte (coaches turned back unlawfully), Lord Atkin’s dissent in Liversidge v Anderson, Article 7 ECHR. Equality before the law: M v Home Office (minister in contempt), R v Chaytor (MPs not protected by privilege), with exceptions for diplomats and the monarch. Fairness and clarity: Evans v Attorney General, Miller and Cherry (prorogation), Anisminic and Privacy International (ouster clauses read narrowly).
caption: Each element is backed by modern cases where the courts held power to account.

after: ## Applying the doctrine to each area
alt: A table for the three areas. Law making: published, prospective statutes and section 19 HRA statements, against retrospective legislation, Henry VIII powers and ouster clauses. The legal system: independent judges, open courts, appeals and juries, against cost, reduced legal aid and delay. Substantive law: offences defined in advance and the presumption of mens rea, against vague common law offences, strict liability and retrospective judicial change.
caption: In each area, show where the doctrine is respected and where it is under strain.

after: ## Applying the doctrine to each area
alt: A balance tipped towards respect for human dignity over the principle of no retrospective liability. In R v R (1991) the House of Lords held a husband could be guilty of raping his wife; in SW v UK (1995) the European Court found no breach of Article 7 because the change was a foreseeable development consistent with human dignity.
caption: One rule of law principle can be outweighed by another value.

alt: Five building blocks of the annotated answer: the core principle of independent courts; equality with M v Home Office; fairness and access to courts with UNISON; Bingham’s sixth principle; and an evaluative point that legal aid cuts leave some unable to enforce rights.
caption: Principle, element and case, second element and case, theory, then evaluation.
